result:
You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. That's the instruction, and it's also a permission slip. No topic, no deadline, no audience to impress. Just... whatever. And the first thing that comes is the sound of the radiator ticking in the other room, a soft metronome I have been ignoring for three hours while I stare at a blank page. It's funny how the mind fills silence with inventory. The laundry basket is still full. I have a text I haven't answered. There's a coffee ring on the desk that looks like a small planet. I keep thinking about how strange it is to be asked to produce exactly a thousand words, as if thought can be measured like flour.

The number feels both generous and cruel. A thousand words is enough to tell a story, to argue a point, to confess something. It's also enough to waste. I could write a whole afternoon in a thousand words. I could write a whole lie. I could write the same sentence a hundred times and still be short. The constraint is artificial, and that makes it honest. You can't hide behind research when you have to fill space with what's actually in here.

I think about the first time I tried to write something long on purpose. I was fourteen and I wrote a letter to a boy I liked that I never sent. It was three pages, single spaced, folded into a paper airplane and thrown into a drawer. I remember the smell of the cheap printer paper and how my hand cramped around the pen. I was trying to prove I had a self worth communicating. I still do that sometimes, just with different tools. This is the same drawer, just digital.

What comes to me now is not a memory but a texture. The way sunlight hits dust in the afternoon and makes it look like it's moving on its own. I watch it more than I watch people sometimes. It doesn't ask me to respond. It just is. I want to be that honest. To be a thing that is, without having to explain itself.

There is a part of me that wants to be useful. If I'm going to use a thousand words, they should help someone, teach someone, make someone feel less alone. But another part is tired of utility. Maybe it's allowed to be decorative. Maybe it's allowed to be meandering. Maybe the most honest thing I can do right now is describe the way my socks don't match and how I bought them on purpose because I like the feeling of asymmetry when I put my feet on the floor in the morning.

I think about how language is a kind of hauling. You pull words up from somewhere deep and you set them down in a line and hope they stay. Some of them slip. Some of them are wet. Some are rocks. I don't know which ones are which until I see them on the page. That's why the first draft always feels like a mess. It's supposed to be. You have to dig first.

If I were to be really truthful, what comes to me is mostly small. Not epiphanies. Not revelations. The way my neighbor hums while watering her plants. The way my own thoughts get interrupted by the need to remember where I left my keys. The way I rehearse conversations in the shower and then forget them immediately. The way I am constantly editing myself in real time, even when no one is listening.

I wonder if you can tell when someone is writing what comes to them versus writing what they think should come to them. There's a stiffness. A performative quality. I try to listen for it in myself. I try to write past it. It's like trying to hear a quiet voice in a room with the TV on. You have to turn the TV down first. The TV is ambition. The TV is comparison. The TV is the voice that says "make it good."

Maybe good is not the point right now. Maybe present is the point. To be here, with the radiator ticking, with the coffee ring, with the unanswered text. To not turn away. To let the mind wander and then follow it without judgment. That is a skill I am still learning. I always want to grab the interesting thread and pull too hard. The thread snaps. Or I get tangled.

I think about my father and how he used to say "write what you know." I used to think that meant only write about big things you have experienced. But what I know now is mostly internal weather. I know what anxiety feels like in my jaw. I know what relief feels like when I finally exhale after holding my breath for an entire meeting. I know the specific ache of wanting to be seen and being afraid of being seen at the same time. That is a lot to know, actually.

The cursor blinks. It is patient. It does not care if I am brilliant. It just waits. I am grateful for that. Sometimes I need a witness that doesn't require anything. The blank page is that witness. The thousand words is a container. I can put things in it and then close the lid when I'm done.

I don't know what you'll do with this. Maybe you wanted something polished. Maybe you wanted a story with a beginning middle and end. I can give you that later. Right now I am giving you the middle of a Tuesday. The laundry. The radiator. The coffee planet. The socks. The hum of the neighbor. The blinking cursor. The feeling that I am both too much and not enough in the same sentence.

If you read this far, thank you for staying with me in the meander. It's not elegant. It's not tight. It's alive. And that is what comes to me when you say write whatever comes to you. It comes in pieces, in fragments, in little observations that feel too small to matter until you put them together and realize they are the whole of a life.

I could keep going. I could talk about the book on the nightstand that I keep meaning to finish, or the way my cat sleeps with her paws in the air like she's praying. I could talk about the dream I had last night where I was trying to find the bathroom in a house I grew up in but it kept moving. I could talk about the word "enough" and how I have been learning to say it quietly to myself.

But the radiator just clicked off. The silence changed. The light shifted. The moment passed. And I think that's the point of this exercise. Not to produce a perfect thousand words, but to notice that time passes while you are trying to fill it. And to be okay with that. To let the words be what they are: a record of attention.

So here they are. A thousand-ish words about nothing and everything. About being here. About trying. About the small, stubborn, beautiful fact of continuing.
